teen.open: Is college still worth what it costs? Sometimes, but not automatically. You have to count the cost, and a trade is a real, honorable option too.
teen.close: So the answer: a degree still pays more on average, but it costs a lot, and a trade pays you while you learn. Jesus was a carpenter. Count the cost of both paths before you sign anything, then work hard at whichever you choose.

senior.open: The title asks whether a degree still justifies its price. The lesson's answer is that it often can, but it is now a decision to be counted soberly, while honest work with the hands stands in full honor before Yahweh.
senior.close: So the question has a measured answer. The degree still pays more on average and the trades pay from the first week; neither path ranks above the other in the Word. Count the cost before the debt (Proverbs 24:27), and do the work heartily, as to the Lord.

wi-biology-walked-back-and-the-word-on-t.reason: Opens with Genesis 2:7 but never says plainly whether the selfish gene was wrong; the answer (research real, worldview claim riding on it wrong, Noble's verdict contested) is buried in Stage 2 interpretation; ends on a sorting skill.
wi-biology-walked-back-and-the-word-on-t.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did the selfish gene get it wrong? The research behind it explained a great deal and still does. What was wrong is the claim that rode in on it: that you are your genes, that purpose is an illusion, that there is no Author. That was never measured. Genesis 2:7 declares a man is two acts, dust and then Yahweh's breath, and no reading of the dust will ever find the breath. He said it first; the science is arriving late.
wi-biology-walked-back-and-the-word-on-t.example: MEASURED, CONTESTED, ILLUSTRATION. Measured: the genome was sequenced, three billion base pairs, a real success; a typical polygenic score detects only about 11% of the people who go on to develop a common disease, at a 5% false-positive rate; water has been known to move at random since 1827. Contested: "neo-Darwinism is dead", one eminent man's verdict that mainstream biology has not conceded. Illustration with a known objection: the improbability calculation, which treats selection as a pure random search. Only the first pile is said without a hedge.
wi-biology-walked-back-and-the-word-on-t.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. So did the selfish gene get it wrong? The science under it was real work, and a fair reader says what it explained. The worldview laid over it was wrong: a person is not a readout of a sequence, because the man was formed of dust and then breathed into (Genesis 2:7). Yet the Word does not stand on this lab dispute, and biology has not proved Yahweh; through faith we understand (Hebrews 11:3). He said it first, so your faith does not move when the argument does, and you can learn genetics with delight instead of dread.

teen.open: Are you just your genes? No. Genes are real and they matter, but the Word says Yahweh formed man from dust and then breathed life into him.
teen.close: So the gene research was real science, but the idea that you are nothing but your DNA was wrong. You are fearfully and wonderfully made (Psalm 139:14). And your faith does not depend on scientists agreeing.

senior.open: The title asks whether the selfish-gene account was wrong. The lesson's answer is that its research was real and fruitful, but the claim that a person is only a sequence was never measured, and Genesis 2:7 had already declared otherwise.
senior.close: So the answer keeps the arrow straight. Honor what the gene-centred science explained, keep the contested verdicts narrow, and do not rest faith on a laboratory dispute. Yahweh formed man of dust and breathed into him; He said it first, and the science arrives late.

wi-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-and-the-nam.reason: Opens on a long Word survey of names, arts and patrons; the answer (Congress named it, no man makes the house for his own name, the rescue is a forecast) is scattered across stages; ends on a Stage 5 skill list.
wi-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-and-the-nam.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Whose name goes on the house? In law, the one Congress gave it: a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change the Kennedy Center's name. In the Word, a benefactor may be honored, but no man's own name is what a house is for, and one name stands over every house (Philippians 2:9). The board's claim that only one patron can rescue it is a forecast, not a finding, and the just weight (Proverbs 11:1) asks you to keep those two apart. Here is how to weigh it.
wi-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-and-the-nam.example: TWO WEIGHTS ON ONE SCALE. In public, the center's leaders spoke of record fundraising: a $23 million Honors, $58 million in thirty days, $130 million in a year. In private, documents showed ticket sales and gifts collapsing after the name went on in December: subscriptions down about 36 percent, and about 43 percent of tickets for typical productions unsold in fall 2025. No audited statement has reconciled the two. A just weight puts both on the same scale. Until it is reconciled, the collapse stays a fact and the rescue stays a hope.
wi-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-and-the-nam.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Whose name goes on the house? The one it was built to carry. Congress named this house in 1964, and a court has said only Congress can change it. The Word lets you honor a benefactor without trusting him (Romans 13:7; Psalms 146:3), forbids a man making his own name the point of the house, and weighs every rescue claim on one scale: the collapse is documented, the rescue is a hope. Pay the workers first (Leviticus 19:13). And over every house, including yours, stands the name above every name (Philippians 2:9).

teen.open: The title asks whose name belongs on a building. The Word says you can thank a giver, but a house is never built to make a man's own name great.
teen.close: So whose name goes on the house? The one it was built for. Honor a giver, but don't trust him like a savior, and remember that the name of Jesus is above every name.

senior.open: The question is whose name belongs on a public house, and how to weigh a board's claim that only one patron can save it. The Word honors benefactors but never lets a man's own name become what the house is for.
senior.close: So the answer is measured and plain. Congress gave this house its name; the rescue claim is a forecast to be weighed on one honest scale, not a finding; and every house finally answers to the name above every name (Philippians 2:9).

wi-apa-2021-apology-and-the-one-blood.reason: Darrell's question (was the repair as loud as the harm?) is weighed only in Stage 2 and the Accountability section, framed as a question to keep asking; ends on a Stage 5 skill list rather than the answer.
wi-apa-2021-apology-and-the-one-blood.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. The apology was signed, but was the repair ever as loud as the harm? The confession is real: on 2021-10-29 the APA's governing council voted to apologize to people of color for its role in promoting racism. But the false ranking was taught for most of a century with the full authority of science, and the Word asks more than words after a wrong: forsaking, recompense with a fifth added, and fruit (Proverbs 28:13; Numbers 5:7; Matthew 3:8). Whether the repair matches the harm is the right question to keep asking.
wi-apa-2021-apology-and-the-one-blood.example: WORDS, THEN THE FIFTH PART. Say a man wronged his neighbor of 100 coins. Under Numbers 5:7 his confession does not close the matter. He returns the 100 and adds a fifth, 20 more, so 120 goes back. Zacchaeus went further and restored fourfold, 400 for 100 (Luke 19:8). That is the Word's picture of a repair louder than the wrong. Hold any apology, an institution's or your own, against that measure.
wi-apa-2021-apology-and-the-one-blood.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Was the repair ever as loud as the harm? The confession was real, by vote and in writing, and you should quote it exactly as written, not as a clip remembers it. But in the Word a confession is where repair begins, not where it ends: forsake the wrong, restore it with the fifth part added, and bear fruit. A repair smaller than the wound is what Jeremiah calls healing the hurt slightly (Jeremiah 6:14). So welcome the apology, keep asking for the fruit without contempt, and remember the Word never needed it: He made of one blood all nations (Acts 17:26).

teen.open: The question is whether a big apology fixed a big wrong. It was a real apology, but the Word says saying sorry is only the start.
teen.close: So was the repair as loud as the harm? Not by words alone. The Word asks for turning away, paying back, and real fruit. Keep asking for that, kindly, and quote the apology exactly.

senior.open: The question is whether a formal apology matched the harm it confessed. The confession was real and adopted by vote; the Word adds that forsaking, recompense, and fruit must follow.
senior.close: So the answer rests on Scripture's own standard. A signed confession is a true beginning and should be quoted accurately; whether the repair matches a century of harm is measured by forsaking, recompense, and fruit (Numbers 5:7; Matthew 3:8).

wi-the-wage-that-no-longer-buys-the-day.reason: Haggai 1:6 frames the answer early but implicitly; the plain answer (pay buys less of the day for six months, and what the Word requires) is spread over many sections; ends on a Stage 5 question, not the answer.
wi-the-wage-that-no-longer-buys-the-day.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a wage still buy the day? For six straight months, prices have risen faster than pay, so the same day's work buys less than it did. The work is real and the pay arrives, but, as Haggai says, it goes into a bag with holes (Haggai 1:6). The Word answers with a just measure, a hire paid in full and on time, and a household that knows its own numbers, without fear and without shrugging. Here is how to weigh it.
wi-the-wage-that-no-longer-buys-the-day.example: WHAT THE BIG NUMBER MEASURES. The 74% in the title is heating oil, compared with a year earlier. Gasoline was up 34% over the year. The top-line rate across the whole index was 3.7%, and the 2027 Social Security raise is 3.6%, figured by a different ruler. Each figure is real, and for a family with a furnace the 74% is not a mood. But it does not mean every price rose 74%. Naming each number for what it measures is the just weight this lesson asks of you first.
wi-the-wage-that-no-longer-buys-the-day.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can a wage still buy the day? Less of it than before, and the Word does not tell you that you are imagining it. Yahweh requires a just measure (Leviticus 19:36) and a hire paid in full, on the day (Leviticus 19:13). So know your own numbers (Proverbs 27:23), pay anyone you hire in full, store in the good months as Joseph did, refuse credit as the first answer (Proverbs 22:7), and ask for this day's bread from a Father who already knows what you need (Matthew 6:11, 32).

teen.open: The question is whether a paycheck still covers a normal day. For six months prices have gone up faster than pay, so it covers less.
teen.close: So can a wage still buy the day? Less than before. Know your real numbers, pay people fairly, don't run to credit, and trust the Father who knows what you need.

senior.open: The question is whether a day's pay still buys a day's needs. For six months running, prices have outpaced wages, and the Word names that a wage put into a bag with holes (Haggai 1:6).
senior.close: So the honest answer is that it buys less than it did. The Word's response is a just measure, a hire paid on the day, a household that knows its numbers and stores in good months, and a heart free of both fear and indifference (Matthew 6:32-33).

wi-higher-ed-aid-2026-and-the-student-in.reason: The plain answer (yes, she is a neighbor in need whatever you think of the policy) only appears in the Stage 2 interpretation; the sorting method sits in Stage 4; ends on a Stage 5 question.
wi-higher-ed-aid-2026-and-the-student-in.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is the student in the gap your neighbor too? Yes. A senior who cannot pay her gap this semester is a neighbor in need, whatever you think of the policy that put her there. The rule changes in the clip are real or really proposed and can be stated plainly; the speaker's verdicts on motive are opinion. The Word asks you to sort the clip honestly, then open your hand anyway (Deuteronomy 15:8; 1 John 3:18).
wi-higher-ed-aid-2026-and-the-student-in.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is the student in the gap your neighbor too? Yes, and the Word does not let the policy argument stand between you and her (James 2:15-16). Say the documented rules plainly, carry the stories as testimony and the motives as opinion, and hear the case for reform at its strongest. Then count the cost of any degree in your own house so no one is sold into bondage for it (Luke 14:28; Proverbs 22:7), and in your church ask what is already in the house and open your hand to the student in front of you.

teen.open: Is a college student with money trouble your neighbor too? Yes. Whatever you think of the new rules, she still needs help.
teen.close: So yes, the student in the gap is your neighbor. Check the facts, plan your own school without big debt, and help the student right in front of you.

senior.open: The question is whether a student caught between aid and tuition is our neighbor. The Word answers yes, whatever one concludes about the policy.
senior.close: So the answer is yes. State the rules accurately and leave motives to Yahweh, plan every degree so it can be finished without bondage, and let the church open its hand to the student already in the gap (Deuteronomy 15:8).

wi-the-way-was-45-minutes-long.reason: Deuteronomy 19:6 answers the Word half early, but which claims hold up is only sorted mid-lesson in Stage 2 (NC documented, Texas disputed, Tennessee not found); ends on a Stage 5 skill note.
wi-the-way-was-45-minutes-long.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which claims hold up? North Carolina A&T students really did walk about 45 minutes to vote after losing their campus site, and Liberty really kept its precinct. The Texas claims did not hold up, the Tennessee claims could not be found, and the motive behind it all is not proven. And what does the Word say about a remedy out of reach? Yahweh counts it as a real wrong: He made the roads to refuge reachable on purpose, because the way is long (Deuteronomy 19:6).
wi-the-way-was-45-minutes-long.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which claims hold up, and what does the Word say? The 45-minute walk in North Carolina is documented; the Texas and Tennessee figures are not, so they are not repeated as fact (Exodus 23:1), and no heart is judged (1 Samuel 16:7). But a right too far to reach is counted by Yahweh as a right denied. The duty to clear the road falls on whoever holds it (Isaiah 57:14). For you that means one thing this week: pick one person whose road is long, and shorten it.

teen.open: Some claims in this video were true and some were not. A 45-minute walk to vote really happened in North Carolina; the Texas and Tennessee claims didn't check out.
teen.close: So keep the true parts and drop the false ones. And remember: Yahweh counts a right that is too far away as a real wrong, so help shorten someone's road.

senior.open: The video mixes claims that hold up with claims that do not. The North Carolina walk is documented; the Texas and Tennessee figures were not supported, and the motive is unproven.
senior.close: So the sorting matters, and so does the Word's ruling. A remedy placed out of reach is counted as a remedy denied (Deuteronomy 19:6); the one who holds the road should clear it, and each of us can shorten one road this week.

wi-the-broken-seal-and-the-sure-foundati.reason: The first paragraph answers (a seal is worth what its holder is worth, while no one else can press it; Yahweh's seal cannot be forged), but the long lesson ends on a Stage 5 checklist, not the answer.
wi-the-broken-seal-and-the-sure-foundati.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your lock only as strong as its key? Yes. A certificate, like a king's seal, is worth exactly what its holder is worth, and only while no one else can press it. Eight weak keys meant eight seals anyone could press. Real security rests on Yahweh, whose seal no one can forge (2 Timothy 2:19), so the calm response is to update, warn, and rest. Here is how the Word shows it.
wi-the-broken-seal-and-the-sure-foundati.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your lock only as strong as its key? Every lock men make is, and this week showed it: eight keys anyone could recover, and watchmen who sounded the warning quickly. So the calm response is the prudent one (Proverbs 27:12): check the warning with its owner, update your devices and any site you keep, warn one neighbor, and then rest. Your real security never rested on a key ceremony. It rests on the foundation that stands sure, sealed by the One who knows His own (2 Timothy 2:19).

teen.open: Is a lock only as strong as its key? Yes. When the keys are weak, the lock fails. But your real safety rests with Yahweh.
teen.close: So yes, every human lock depends on its key. Update your stuff, warn a friend, then relax, because Yahweh keeps what is His.

senior.open: The question is whether any lock is stronger than its key. It is not: a seal is worth what its holder is worth. Real security rests on Yahweh, whose seal cannot be forged.
senior.close: So every seal men make is only as strong as its key, and this one failed. The calm answer is to update, warn a neighbor, and then rest, because the foundation Yahweh laid stands sure (2 Timothy 2:19).
